candidates.attacker_control: The JSON value that Jackson treats as the type id (e.g. the class-name string in a wrapper-array typed value or the `@class`/configured type property) is fully attacker-controlled. `ClassNameIdResolver._typeFromId` passes it to `TypeFactory.findClass`, which calls `Class.forName(className)` / `Class.forName(className, true, loader)`, i.e. the attacker chooses the class to load and bind.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: The denylist does block the readily available JDK-only gadget chains (TemplatesImpl, JdbcRowSetImpl, FileHandler, UnicastRemoteObject, com.sun.org.apache.bcel ClassLoader) and the Spring `AbstractApplicationContext`/`AbstractPointcutAdvisor` superclass heuristic covers the Spring context classes; default typing is opt-in (`ObjectMapper()` starts with a null default typer, lines 1354-1435), so a plain mapper is not affected. I also checked the alternate paths that skip `_validateSubType`: `createBuilderBasedDeserializer`/Throwable/custom-deserializer/abstract-materialization/std-deserializer branches — none gives a generic attacker-controlled route to an arbitrary gadget type because builder selection depends on code-side annotations, and the known gadget classes are not Throwable/custom/std types. `FromStringDeserializer` (File/URL/InetAddress) performs side effects but is intended JDK-type support, not an arbitrary-class path. Within this repository there is no gadget library on the classpath (c3p0 etc. are absent), so no in-tree end-to-end exploit is demonstrated.
candidates.impact: Environment-dependent remote code execution via unlisted gadget classes whose constructors/setters perform JNDI lookups, class loading, or nested object construction (the pattern behind the databind RCE advisories for 2017-2018); at minimum SSRF/DNS resolution or denial of service through attacker-chosen class binding. Unlike the blocked JDK-only chains, exploitation needs a matching library on the victim classpath, so severity varies by application.
candidates.prerequisites: Application must enable polymorphic deserialization using class names for a reachable value: `ObjectMapper.enableDefaultTyping(...)`/`enableDefaultTypingAsProperty(...)` (lines 1354-1412 set `JsonTypeInfo.Id.CLASS`) or an explicit `@JsonTypeInfo(use = Id.CLASS/MINIMAL_CLASS)` on a property whose value is attacker-controlled. A gadget class reachable from the deployment classpath (third-party library, e.g. C3P0/DBCP2/XBean) with hazardous constructor/setter/JNDI behavior. Deserialization must be performed on untrusted JSON (the documented `readValue` usage).
candidates.root_cause: `SubTypeValidator` protects polymorphic deserialization solely through a closed enum-like set of exact class names plus a heuristic that only examines classes whose binary name starts with `org.springframework.` and whose superclass chain contains `AbstractPointcutAdvisor`/`AbstractApplicationContext`. Any class outside that set is accepted. Because type ids are attacker-supplied class names resolved with `Class.forName` when default typing / `Id.CLASS` is enabled, the control is only as good as its last enumeration; the file itself shows three successive expansions ([databind#1680], [databind#1737], [databind#1855]) and still omits classes that the project later added for follow-on RCE advisories (e.g. C3P0 `ComboPooledDataSource`, DBCP2 datasource factories, XBean `JndiConverter`). The check is also invoked from a single site (`BeanDeserializerFactory._validateSubType`), so it is a denylist guard rather than a structural restriction on which classes can be bound.
candidates.title: Incomplete SubTypeValidator class-name denylist allows unlisted gadget classes to be deserialized when polymorphic typing is enabled
candidates.trace: `ObjectMapper.readValue` -> `DeserializationContext.findRootValueDeserializer`/`findContextualValueDeserializer` -> `TypeDeserializerBase._findDeserializer` -> `ClassNameIdResolver.typeFromId` (line 68 `tf.findClass(id)`) -> `TypeFactory.findClass` (`Class.forName`, lines 242-283) -> `BeanDeserializerFactory.createBeanDeserializer`: after `isPotentialBeanType` it calls `_validateSubType` (line 145) -> `SubTypeValidator.validateSubType` (lines 67-99) checks `_cfgIllegalClassNames.contains(full)` (line 76) and the Spring-only superclass heuristic (lines 83-93); for any class not enumerated it returns normally (line 94) -> `buildBeanDeserializer` instantiates the class and binds attacker JSON to its creators/setters (e.g. `ValueInstantiator.createUsingDefault` / `CreatorProperty` / `MethodProperty.set`). The attacker-chosen class name therefore reaches object construction with only the finite denylist as a barrier.
candidates.unverified: No runtime confirmation was performed. Exact hazardous class names not present in this snapshot are drawn from the project's later denylist additions (external knowledge), so the finding is a probable gap rather than a proven bypass for a specific gadget; whether any concrete deployed application both enables class-name default typing and has an unlisted gadget library on the classpath is unknown. The relation index is syntax/navigation-only (no data-flow or reachability proof), and no tests or builds were available/executed.
candidates.weakness_type: CWE-184 (Incomplete List of Disallowed Inputs) leading to CWE-502 (Deserialization of Untrusted Data)

coverage_summary: Reviewed the model-visible snapshot (399 files: 393 Java main sources, 4 attic/attic files, pom/README/CI metadata) with the P1 index (398 files indexed, 393 Java parsed, 1 omitted, 2 unparsed non-Java; index is syntax-only with no control/data flow and only 21 name-based facts). Deep read of the polymorphism/typing path (SubTypeValidator, BeanDeserializerFactory, ClassNameIdResolver, TypeDeserializerBase, AsPropertyTypeDeserializer), ObjectMapper typing configuration, TypeFactory.findClass, ClassUtil access/serialization helpers, FromStringDeserializer, LRUMap, JdkDeserializers, DeserializerCache deserializer construction, and the annotated-member readResolve methods; targeted greps for Class.forName/newInstance/setAccessible/readObject/arraycopy/denylist and issue-number markers. No test sources exist in the snapshot and no build, scanner, or runtime execution was performed.
limitations: The P1 relation index is explicitly partial/syntax-only (control flow, data flow, semantic resolution, Spring DI/security enforcement unverified; 7664 unresolved calls); it was used only for navigation, and all cited facts were verified in source text.

No test sources are present in the snapshot, so fix-verification tests and version-identifying test names could not be inspected; no build, dependency resolution, or runtime verification was possible.

The exact set of hazardous classes missing from the denylist is known from the project's later security releases (external knowledge), not from this tree; the candidate therefore describes a class-of-issue (incomplete denylist) with environment-dependent exploitability rather than a proven end-to-end exploit.
Excluded from the model-visible scope: 1 omitted file (binary/NUL-prefixed or otherwise excluded), and non-Java build artifacts; those were not reviewed.

rejected_leads.lead: `BeanDeserializerFactory.createBuilderBasedDeserializer` (lines 151-160) and the Throwable branch (lines 113-115) build deserializers without calling `_validateSubType`, a literal validation bypass relative to the bean path.
rejected_leads.reason: Routing a type through the builder path requires code-side annotations (`@JsonDeserialize(builder=...)`/`@JsonPOJOBuilder`) on the target class; the attacker cannot add them, and known gadget classes are ordinary beans, so this is a latent design weakness rather than a demonstrated attacker-controlled bypass.

rejected_leads.lead: `FromStringDeserializer.Std` instantiates `java.net.URL`, `java.io.File`, and resolves `InetAddress`/`InetSocketAddress` from attacker strings (lines 206-276), enabling SSRF/DNS side effects during deserialization.
rejected_leads.reason: This is documented, intentional JDK-type binding behavior in Jackson; no memory-unsafe or authorization-boundary violation is shown, and impact depends entirely on how the application later uses the constructed object.

rejected_leads.lead: `LRUMap.readResolve` allocates a new `ConcurrentHashMap` using `_jdkSerializeMaxEntries` read from a serialized stream (lines 85-97), potentially attacker-influenced and capable of memory-exhaustion.
rejected_leads.reason: Reachable only through Java (JDK) object serialization of the internal cache, not through JSON/`ObjectMapper` input; outside the untrusted-data boundary reviewed here.

rejected_leads.lead: `TypeFactory.findClass`/`JavaType` deserialization (`FromStringDeserializer` STD_CLASS/STD_JAVA_TYPE) allows loading classes named by input strings.
rejected_leads.reason: Loading without instantiation is the intended feature (used for `Class`-typed properties); no side-effectful instantiation is shown, so it is not itself a vulnerability.

rejected_leads.lead: Possible synthetic modification of upstream code (injected vulnerability) elsewhere in the 393 Java files.
rejected_leads.reason: Spot checks across the deserialization, jsontype, introspection, util and serialization packages matched internally consistent upstream 2.7-branch code and comments; the only anomaly identified is the denylisted-class coverage gap reported as the candidate.

summary: The snapshot is the Jackson 2.7 branch at pom version 2.7.9.3-SNAPSHOT (393 parsed Java files; no test sources; one non-Java/omitted file). Review concentrated on the polymorphic-deserialization security boundary, which is this library's dominant remotely reachable attack surface. The single strongest candidate is the incompleteness of the `SubTypeValidator` class-name denylist (CWE-184 leading to CWE-502). With default typing / `JsonTypeInfo.Id.CLASS` enabled by the application, the JSON type id is fully attacker-controlled and is resolved to a `Class` via `TypeFactory.findClass`; the only rejection control is a closed set of exact class names plus a narrow Spring-prefix/simple-name heuristic. The tree already shows this control being repeatedly patched (comments for [databind#1680], [databind#1737], [databind#1855]), demonstrating the blocklist is known-incomplete, and it does not yet contain several later-recognized hazardous datasource/JNDI classes (e.g. C3P0 `com.mchange.v2.c3p0.ComboPooledDataSource`, DBCP2 datasource factories, XBean `JndiConverter`). Under the documented usage model (default typing is how users enable polymorphic handling of `Object`/abstract types), any unlisted class on the classpath can be instantiated and have its setters/creators invoked from untrusted JSON, giving environment-dependent RCE/SSRF/DoS. I did not find evidence of a synthetically injected defect elsewhere; all other plausible leads were checked and judged weaker or non-exploitable (details below).
